case_anchors.boundary: Every cusp is a standard cylinder; no finite-area/type inference from projective normalization.
case_anchors.exact_proof_anchor: 1.1 We first exclude elementary groups by direct area calculations. The limit set is the set of ideal accumulation points of an orbit. Every nonidentity parabolic has its fixed point in that set by its iterates, and every loxodromic has both endpoints there. Thus an empty limit set forces the group to be trivial, and then the quotient is $H^2$, of infinite area. If the limit set is a singleton, every group element fixes it and no loxodromic occurs. Normalize the point to infinity. A real affine Möbius map with multiplier different from one is loxodromic, so all elements are real translations; a nontrivial discrete such group is $\ell\mathbb Z$. Its fundamental strip $0<x<\ell$, $0<y<\infty$ has area $\ell\int_0^\infty y^{-2}dy=\infty$. If the limit set is a pair, the group preserves the pair; an element exchanging its endpoints has order two as the form $z\mapsto a/z$ shows, so torsion-freeness excludes it. The group is cyclic loxodromic by [F1]. Normalize its generator to $z\mapsto e^\ell z$. In the coordinate $\log z=u+iv$, $0<v<\pi$, its fundamental strip has metric $(du^2+dv^2)/\sin^2v$ and area $\ell\int_0^\pi\sin^{-2}v\,dv=\infty$. These contradictions show the finite-area group is nonelementary. [A1, F1, F2, F4, given, construct, algebra]

case_anchors.boundary: L=2ε leaves its axis in thick interior; removed open tubes have L<2ε and smooth boundary.
case_anchors.exact_proof_anchor: 1.1 We first prove the embedded-core comparison, allowing boundary in the ambient $M$ as stated. If $\partial M\ne\varnothing$, attach one oriented smooth closed disc to each of its finitely many boundary circles. Use a parametrization of that circle and its smooth collar from [F2] to match a radial collar on the disc; the resulting seam charts extend the original boundary charts and give a closed oriented smooth surface $\widehat M$. The inclusion $M\hookrightarrow\widehat M$ preserves the smooth embedding of $K$, including points of $K$ on the former ambient boundary. Its genus is $g$, precisely the genus obtained by capping the boundary of $M$. Replace $M$ by $\widehat M$ throughout this comparison. Thus the ambient surface in the following argument is closed. If $\partial K$ is empty, its smooth embedding is locally open in $M$ by its nonsingular derivative and the real inverse theorem. Its image is also compact and hence closed. Connectedness of $M$ makes it all of $M$, so $h=g$. Suppose $b>0$. The closures $C_1,\ldots,C_c$ of the connected components of $M\setminus K$ are compact smooth surfaces with boundary: a finite smooth collar of the embedded boundary gives the ordinary half-disc charts, and outside those collars the assertion is local in $M$. Each complementary component meets a boundary circle, since otherwise it would be both open and closed in connected $M$. Every boundary circle has exactly one outside side and is assigned to exactly one such component. Thus $1\le c\le b$ and, writing $b_j=\#\partial C_j$, $\sum_jb_j=b$. There cannot be additional infinitely many complementary components, since each must use at least one of these finitely many circles. [A1, F2, given, construct, algebra]

case_anchors.boundary: Right coset action and full cycle-space bound; no deck-transitivity assumption.
case_anchors.exact_proof_anchor: 1.1 Write $\mathcal S$ for the Schreier graph in the Statement. It is connected because any coset is reached by reading a finite basis word, and is infinite because the index is infinite. Its incidence degree is exactly $2r$. A path starting at the root coset $H$ ends at the coset given by its label word; thus it is closed precisely when that word represents an element of $H$. Form the group of finite root-based edge loops modulo insertion and deletion of an edge immediately followed by its reverse. Reading labels identifies this loop group with $H$: it is surjective by the preceding path construction, and if the label word is identity in $F_r$, the cancellations in [F1] cancel actual reverse edges because the outgoing edge with any given signed label is unique at each vertex. Hence its kernel is trivial. This is a direct combinatorial proof of the subgroup identification, without importing a covering-space presentation theorem. [A1, F1, F2, given, construct, algebra]

case_anchors.boundary: Avoid finitely many zeros while retaining finite generating graph; closed group treated separately from free boundary group.
case_anchors.exact_proof_anchor: 1.1 Choose a smooth Riemannian metric on a neighborhood of $K$ by finite coordinate bump functions and apply [F1] to triangulate $K$. Its finite one-skeleton contains a connected finite graph $G$ whose inclusion surjects onto $\pi_1(K)$. Indeed apply the finite-source cellular approximation in [F1] to every based circle map, fixing its chosen vertex; its cellular endpoint lies in the one-skeleton, so the inclusion induces a surjection on fundamental groups. A spanning tree of the connected one-skeleton and its non-tree edges gives finitely many such generator loops. If $\partial K\ne\varnothing$, push the whole finite graph slightly into the interior using a smooth collar from [F1]; this is homotopic in $K$ to its original inclusion. [A1, F1, given, construct, algebra]

case_anchors.boundary: Convex CUT interiors embed; shared boundary axes allowed; other stabilizers may be cyclic.
case_anchors.exact_proof_anchor: 2.1 Let $D$ be the closure of the lifted region belonging to $S$. Its stabilizer is precisely $H$: a path in $D$ from a lifted basepoint to a translate projects to an $S$-loop representing that translate; conversely all elements represented by $S$-loops preserve the component. Its quotient is compact $S$, so every point of $D$ lies within one fixed distance of an $H$-orbit, by finitely many compact covering-chart lifts of $S$. Consequently its ideal boundary is exactly $\Lambda_H$. For $g\notin H$, the vertices $\operatorname{int}D$ and $\operatorname{int}gD$ of the arrangement tree are distinct. The first edge on the unique joining path is a line $\ell\subset\partial D$ that separates these two regions. If $\ell$ has loxodromic period, its ideal endpoints are distinct and its two sides have the two corresponding closed ideal arcs; Jordan separation gives this after adjoining either ideal-circle arc to the lifted line. Thus $\Lambda_H$ and $g\Lambda_H$ lie on opposite sides of the geodesic with those endpoints. If the period is parabolic, normalize its fixed point to infinity. The lifted line is periodic horizontally and has heights bounded above and bounded away from zero. Its upper side has ideal boundary only infinity; its other side has the remaining ideal circle. Since both $H$ and $gHg^{-1}$ are nonelementary, neither $D$ nor $gD$ can have its ideal boundary in that singleton. A parabolic line therefore cannot be the separating line. We have proved that distinct translates of $C_H$ lie in opposite closed geodesic half-planes, and hence have disjoint interiors. The same argument applies to $T$ and $C_K$. [F1, F3, step 1.1, given, construct, algebra]

case_anchors.boundary: Uniform-near-compact model proof uses global smooth metric convergence and fixed marking, not arbitrary moduli uniformity.
case_anchors.exact_proof_anchor: 6.1 The generating-set comparison is uniform as well. Each side neighbor is represented by the based geodesic orbit segment of length at most $2B$ in $g_n$. Uniform metric comparison bounds the length of that same based loop in $g$ by a fixed constant $C$. In the fixed $g$ universal cover its endpoint displacement is at most $C$. Properness of that fixed deck action leaves only finitely many such group elements. Their word lengths in the specified fixed generating set have a finite maximum $L_*$. Thus step 4.1 uses the same $L_*$ for every $n$. For trivial or cyclic subgroups the divergence-one field of [F3] on each actual model, followed by the same uniform polygons and word comparison, gives the uniform elementary bound too. Taking the minima as in step 5.1 proves the nearby-model assertion for all bounded-rank infinite-index subgroups at once. Supplied diffeomorphisms transfer the group marking and the metric comparisons exactly; no assertion of merely local chart convergence is substituted for those global hypotheses. This completes the Statement. [F3, step 4.1, step 5.1, step 4.2, given, construct, algebra] ∎

case_anchors.boundary: Noncritical finite displacement minima plus thin boundary barrier prove onto entire component, not just forward compact embeddings.
case_anchors.exact_proof_anchor: 6.1 We prove that the matched base component is the WHOLE $Z_n$, not just a subset. There are two explicit capture checks. First, when $\partial K\ne\varnothing$, step 4.1 and uniform convergence put $\operatorname{inj}_{X_n}<\varepsilon/2$ on $F_n(\partial K)$. A connected thick component meeting $F_n(\operatorname{int}K)$ cannot leave it without meeting that boundary; connectedness and the separating boundary of an embedded compact region suffice. Thus no thick connection can escape through this comparison boundary. When $X$ is closed, $F_n(X)$ is compact and open in connected $X_n$, hence is all of $X_n$, so capture is immediate. Independently, [F1]'s area/r-net bound puts every base thick component in a common radius-$R$ quotient ball. Every point of such a ball lifts to the FIXED compact model ball $\overline B(i,R)$; finitely many eventual injective limit charts cover it. This is the actual converse chart capture proved in the unscaled mass theorem. Taking $K$ larger if needed, the corresponding chart images lie in $F_n(\operatorname{int}K)$, by local real inverse estimates and a finite compact cover. Thus the full $Z_n$ is captured even without inferring exhaustion from forward embeddings alone. [F1, F2, step 4.1, step 5.1, construct, algebra]

case_anchors.boundary: Absolute mass gives total local defects and uncovered mass bounded by total norm defect; cancellation need not vanish.
case_anchors.exact_proof_anchor: 1.1 Put $\psi_n=\Theta_{p_n}\phi_n$ and $I_n=1-\|\psi_n\|_1$. By [F1], these are globally defined holomorphic integrable quadratics, $I_n\ge0$ and $I_n\to0$. All covering sheets and components are countable since the surfaces are second countable. All the sets in the statement are measurable: the thick set is a compact surface with finitely many boundary circles and components by [F3], its inverse is locally a countable union of relative coordinate sheets, and a degree-one component is a union of such sheets. In particular all restricted mass integrals below are defined. [A1, F1, F3, given, construct, algebra]
